paras: The attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford took place on Sunday, February 12, 1882, when a crowd of about fifty went to the jail at Gainesville, Texas, intending to seize Alford, a Black music teacher accused of attempting to rape a fourteen-year-old girl. The crowd confined itself to talk and threats and withdrew when the jail guards refused it, and Alford remained in custody to await trial. The episode is known from a single item in the Waco Daily Examiner, which quoted the Gainesville Hesperian.

Alford had worked as a barber and music teacher in Waco, where, according to the Examiner, he styled himself "Majah Alford." After leaving Waco he taught band music and dancing in different parts of the state. At Gainesville he was charged with attempting to rape a fourteen-year-old girl of his class and was jailed.

According to the Hesperian, on that Sunday "a crowd numbering perhaps fifty or more went to the jail with the avowed intention" of taking him. The paper wrote that the crowd's demonstrations were "confined to talk and theats" and that the guards' refusal "was taken quite submissively." The Examiner credited the guards, who "could not be intimidated," with preventing a "necktie picnic."
Alford was still in custody when the Examiner wrote. No report of a trial or verdict was found in the coverage.

The Gainesville Hesperian, as quoted, appealed to the "good, solid sense of the would-be avengers" and asked that the accused be given a fair trial. It argued that "lynch law" would be a "lasting disgrace" to the city and injure its prospects, while calling the alleged crime "one of the most heinous known to man." The Waco Daily Examiner framed the same passage differently, heading it "Beastly 'Majah' Alford" and calling him "this beast." Its introduction mocked Alford's speech in dialect, said he had been "far too forward with those he could in no wise approach in rank or station," and joked that if convicted he would "do some dancing himself."
The Examiner item, published on Friday, February 17, is the only report of the episode that was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford
bases: A crowd of fifty or more went to the Gainesville jail with the 'avowed intention' of seizing a Black prisoner accused of attempted rape and was turned away by the guards (A1).

No one was killed: the crowd's demonstrations were 'confined to talk and theats' and it withdrew when the guards refused it (A1); the episode is an attempted lynching by a group of about fifty acting on an accusation of attempted rape.
The only report is the Waco Daily Examiner's item (A1), which rests on a quoted passage from the Gainesville Hesperian; no independent account was found.

accounts.label: Gainesville Hesperian (as quoted)
accounts.gist: On Sunday a crowd of perhaps fifty or more went to the jail to take Alford, but confined itself to talk and threats and submissively accepted the guards' refusal; the paper urged a fair trial and warned against lynch law.

accounts.label: Waco Daily Examiner
accounts.gist: Introduced the Hesperian passage with a mocking sketch of Alford's career at Waco, said he was lucky the guards could not be intimidated, and predicted punishment if the charge were proved.

framing.detail: The Examiner's own text ('Beastly "Majah" Alford', 'this beast', 'necktie picnic') treated the accusation as settled and the near-lynching as a joke, while the Hesperian passage it quoted opposed lynch law and asked for a fair trial.

quotes: Last Sunday it was fortunate for this beast that the guards at the jail could not be intimidated, or he might have been the principal actor at a necktie picnic.
On Sunday last a crowd numbering perhaps fifty or more went to the jail with the avowed intention of taking possession of the "Majah's" precious caress.
Happily their demonstrations were confined to talk and theats, and a stand-off from the guards was taken quite submissively.
To allow "lynch law" to have full scope in a city of our retensions would be a lasting disgrace and work incalculable injury to its prospects
was far too forward with those he could in no wise approach in rank or station.
